newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's generals sap Islamist coalition.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's generals sap Islamist coalition.

text.p: Turkey's armed forces, vanguard of the secular establishment, have brought the Islamist-led government to the brink of collapse with a carefully calibrated campaign so far untainted by threats of direct intervention.

Analysts say the generals have steadily increased the pressure on the Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, modern Turkey's first Islamist leader, while paying lip service to the need for a "political" solution to end his 10-month tenure.
Favoured weapons include strategic leaks to the media to embarrass the Islamists and discreet alliances with officials in the courts, the police and elsewhere in the secular power structure.
One local gendarme commander was captured on video denouncing Erbakan as a "pimp" for accepting Saudi hospitality during the Moslem haj pilgrimage.

"The army have been effective in undermining this government, but they have been careful to base their arguments in law against rising Islamist activism," political commentator Ismet Berkan told Reuters.

So far the brass have remained content to use the National Security Council -- a body they dominate -- to put pressure on Erbakan to curtail anti-secular activities on the part of his core constituents. Few are talking openly of a coup d'etat.

But lurking in the background is the universal conviction the army retains the will and the power to do what it has done three times since 1960 -- depose a civilian government it felt was threatening the stability of the republic.
The political war of attrition is taking its toll on Erbakan, who has been unable to implement the Islam-based, millenarian "Just Order" he promised his voters.
"It is being demolished by instalments," said the daily Radikal in a front-page headline, summing up the prospects for the Erbakan government at the hands of the generals.

At the weekend two cabinet ministers from the conservative wing of the coalition resigned, with talk of more defections to come from secularists uneasy with the direction of the country under Erbakan.
"Turkey has turned into a country that does not know where it is going internationally," Yalim Erez, outgoing minister for trade and industry, said in announcing his resignation.
"It has yet to choose between East and West."
An eight-hour meeting of the Security Council ended late on Saturday with Erbakan making broad concessions to army demands for a crackdown on what it sees as the creeping Islamisation of public life.
But the younger leaders in his Welfare Party are already challenging their leader -- known widely as Hoca, or teacher -- and demanding fresh polls rather than retreat on social policy.

The military's tactics have been dictated by the lack of effective opposition to the Islamists, who exploited divisions among the secularist parties to parlay a plurality of 21 percent in general elections into their first real hold on power.
"The army is the determining factor in pushing the government to the edge," said analyst Cengiz Candar.
"But if we had a system with real parties, this stage would have been achieved by the opposition. The military has taken over the role of opposition," Candar said in an interview.

Now this same lack of effective secularist opposition -- which collectively won more than 75 percent in the latest general elections -- is complicating the search for a solution to Turkey's political woes.

Petty rivalries divide the leaders of two conservative parties, which broadly share the same platforms and outlooks. One, the True Path Party of U.S.-educated economist Tansu Ciller who was Turkey's first woman prime minister, preferred coalition with Erbakan's Islamists.
Likewise, the remnants of Turkey's once-proud left are riven with personal disputes, and the recent death of Alperslan Turkes has left a gaping hole among the ultra-nationalists.
As a result, the armed forces have stepped into the breach, making political demands while avoiding a final showdown.
But is it a coup?
"That depends on your definition," said Candar. "I think this is not a coup like (the three before), but the military remains just as effective in the political arena."
